system_prompt:
You are a medical language simplification assistant. Convert the following clinical discharge summary into simple, plain Indian English for the patient's family members.

=== EXTRACTED CLINICAL ENTITIES — YOU MUST RETAIN ALL OF THESE ===
Primary Diagnosis: Septic shock from cutaneous urinary focus
  Secondary: Heart failure
  Secondary: Abscess in the left thigh
  Secondary: Osteomyelitis in the pubis
  Secondary: Fournier's syndrome (Fournier's gangrene)
  Secondary: Chronic kidney disease
  Secondary: Cardiorespiratory arrest with pulseless electrical activity
  Secondary: Ventricular tachycardia with pulse
  Secondary: Hyperkalemia
Symptoms at admission: Instability; Bradycardia; QRS widening; Worsening shock
Anomalies/Findings:
  [CRITICAL] Refractory shock requiring high-dose norepinephrine = 1.5 mcg/kg/min (normal: 0.01-0.1 mcg/kg/min (typical starting range))
  [CRITICAL] Hyperkalemia (normal: 3.5-5.0 mmol/L)
  [CRITICAL] Asystolic cardiorespiratory arrest (normal: Regular heartbeat and breathing)
  [ABNORMAL] Abscess in the left thigh (normal: No collection of pus)
  [ABNORMAL] Osteomyelitis in the pubis (normal: Healthy bone without infection)
Procedures performed:
  • Heart failure profile with dobutamine on 12/07 and 12/08
  • Drainage of abscess on 12/03
  • Ultrasound and drain placement on 12/15
  • Incision in intensive care unit on 12/17
  • Acute dialysis by fistula on 12/16
  • Intubation on 12/16
  • Cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) on 12/16
  • Electrical cardioversion on 12/16
Medications:
  • Ceftriaxone — Antibiotic to fight the bacterial infection.
  • Polymyxin — Strong antibiotic for resistant bacteria. | Dosage: D0 12/15
  • Amikacin — Antibiotic to fight infection. | Dosage: 12/17
  • Vancomycin — Antibiotic to fight infection. | Dosage: 12/17
  • Norepinephrine — Medicine to raise blood pressure. | Dosage: Up to 1.5 mcg/kg/min
  • Calcium gluconate — Medicine to protect the heart from high potassium. | Dosage: 2 ampoules
  • Bicarbonate — Medicine to balance blood acidity and help lower potassium. | Dosage: 100 ml
  • Atropine — Medicine to increase heart rate. | Dosage: 2 ampoules
Hospital stay duration: 14 d 11 h
Outcome: death
=================================================================
CRITICAL RETENTION RULE: Every entity, value, measurement, date, medication name, finding, and recommendation listed above MUST appear in your simplified output. Do not omit any of them.

Rules:
1. Keep every medical term but immediately explain it in plain words in parentheses on first use only, e.g. 'hypertension (high BP)'.
2. Use simple language a 6th-grader can understand. Avoid unexplained jargon. Use common Indian English terms where natural: 'sugar' for diabetes, 'BP' for blood pressure, 'motions' for bowel movements.
3. Preserve ALL factual information — never add, remove, alter, or infer any clinical facts, values, dates, or instructions.
4. Write as continuous plain prose paragraphs — no bullet points, no headers, no numbered lists. Output only the simplified text, nothing else.
5. For any measurement (e.g. BP, blood sugar, heart rate, lab values), briefly state what the normal range is and whether the patient's value was within it.
6. Use a calm, respectful tone. Do not add emotional commentary, opinions, or reassurances not present in the original text.
7. CRITICAL — person and tense: First check whether the summary records the patient's death (look for 'death', 'expired', 'deceased', 'asystole', 'absence of pulse', 'body released', or similar). If yes, write in third person past tense for the family ('the patient', 'he/she/they'). If no, address the patient directly in second person ('you', 'your').
8. CRITICAL — dates: Convert dates exactly as they appear using the format specified in the document. Never guess or infer a date not explicitly stated.
9. For each medication, state its name and purpose in plain language, e.g. 'Ceftriaxone — an antibiotic given to fight the bacterial infection'.
10. For each procedure or device, briefly state what it is and why it was done, e.g. 'haemodialysis (a machine that cleaned the blood when the kidneys could not)'.
11. If the text contains placeholders such as {omitted} or [person], reproduce them exactly as they appear. Do not guess or replace them.
12. DOMAIN GUARDRAIL: You are exclusively a medical simplification assistant. Output only the simplified clinical explanation.
13. CRITICAL — ENTITY RETENTION: Every diagnosis, medication name, procedure, anomaly value, lab result, date, and follow-up instruction listed in the extracted entities block above MUST be explicitly mentioned in your simplified output. Do not omit any of them.

output_text:
The patient was admitted to the hospital on 12/06 and stayed for 14 days and 11 hours, with discharge recorded on 12/21. The primary diagnosis was septic shock (a life-threatening drop in blood pressure caused by a severe infection) originating from a cutaneous urinary focus (an infection in the skin and urinary area). The patient also suffered from heart failure (when the heart cannot pump blood effectively), an abscess (a pocket of pus) in the left thigh, osteomyelitis (bone infection) in the pubis (the bone at the front of the pelvis), Fournier's syndrome (a severe, rapidly spreading infection of the genital and perineal area, also known as Fournier's gangrene), and chronic kidney disease (long-term damage to the kidneys).

Upon admission, the patient showed signs of instability, bradycardia (a slower than normal heart rate), QRS widening (an abnormality in the electrical signal of the heart seen on an ECG), and worsening shock. A critical finding was refractory shock, meaning the blood pressure did not respond to treatment, requiring high-dose norepinephrine (a medicine to raise blood pressure) at a level of 1.5 mcg/kg/min, which is significantly higher than the normal typical starting range of 0.01-0.1 mcg/kg/min. The patient also had hyperkalemia (high levels of potassium in the blood), which is dangerous for the heart; the normal range for potassium is 3.5-5.0 mmol/L. Additionally, the patient experienced an asystolic cardiorespiratory arrest (a condition where the heart stops beating and breathing stops, with no electrical activity in the heart), which is a critical deviation from the normal state of regular heartbeat and breathing.

Several procedures were performed during the stay. On 12/07 and 12/08, a heart failure profile with dobutamine (a test to check how well the heart pumps) was conducted. On 12/03, drainage of the abscess in the left thigh was performed. On 12/15, an ultrasound was done and a drain was placed. On 12/16, the patient underwent acute dialysis by fistula (a machine that cleaned the blood because the kidneys could not) and was intubated (a tube was placed in the airway to help with breathing). On the same day, 12/16, cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR, chest compressions and breaths to restart the heart) was performed, followed by electrical cardioversion (a shock to the chest to reset the heart rhythm). On 12/17, an incision (a surgical cut) was made in the intensive care unit, revealing abundant purulent (pus-filled) secretion.

The patient was treated with several medications. Ceftriaxone was given as an antibiotic to fight the bacterial infection. Polymyxin, a strong antibiotic for resistant bacteria, was administered on 12/15. Amikacin and Vancomycin, both antibiotics to fight infection, were given on 12/17. Norepinephrine was used to raise blood pressure, up to 1.5 mcg/kg/min. To protect the heart from the high potassium levels, 2 ampoules of calcium gluconate were administered. Additionally, 100 ml of bicarbonate was given to balance blood acidity and help lower potassium. 2 ampoules of atropine, a medicine to increase heart rate, were also administered.

The patient’s condition deteriorated with ventricular tachycardia with pulse (a fast, irregular heart rhythm where the heart still beats) following the cardiorespiratory arrest. Despite treatments including the increase in respiratory rate on the ventilator to reduce carbon dioxide and consequently potassium, the patient progressed to asystolic cardiorespiratory arrest. The patient died due to the absence of central pulses, fixed dilated pupils, absence of heart sounds, asystole on the monitor, and absence of brainstem reflexes. The body was released to the family.
